title: We Got Better at Keeping You Alive. Not at Keeping Healthy.
excerpt: Global life expectancy keeps rising. Healthy life expectancy is not keeping pace, and the gap between the two has widened in 203 of 204 countries since 1990.
content_html:
Global life expectancy keeps rising. Healthy life expectancy is not keeping pace, and the gap between the two has widened in 203 of 204 countries since 1990.

Living longer gets treated as an unambiguous win. The newest global health data says a growing share of those extra years are sick years, and the gap between how long people live and how long they stay healthy is getting worse, not better.

Researchers call it the morbidity gap: life expectancy minus healthy life expectancy, the years a person can expect to live free of serious disease or disability. Global life expectancy rose from 64.6 to 73.8 years between 1990 and 2023. Healthy life expectancy rose too, but slower, from 55.9 to 63.1 years. The difference, years spent sick rather than dead or healthy, grew from 8.8 to 10.7 years, an increase of nearly 22 percent.

That is not a rounding error in one unlucky country. The gap widened in 203 of 204 countries and territories studied, and across the whole adult lifespan rather than only its final years.

  • Share of a global lifetime spent in poor health rose from 13.6 percent in 1990 to 14.5 percent in 2023
  • Women carry a wider gap than men, 12.1 years in poor health on average against 9.3 years
  • The three widest national gaps in 2023 belonged to rich countries: the United States at 14 years, Australia at 13.9, and Canada at 13.7

The cause is not a handful of rare diseases. Musculoskeletal disorders led by low back pain, depression and anxiety, age related hearing loss, falls, and a cluster of other chronic, non fatal conditions together account for 57 percent of all unhealthy years worldwide. Modern medicine is very good at keeping someone alive through a heart attack, a cancer diagnosis, or a stroke. It is much less good at preventing the chronic condition that settles in afterward and stays for good.

In 1980 the physician James Fries proposed the opposite outcome. His compression of morbidity hypothesis predicted that healthy habits would push back the onset of illness faster than they pushed back death, squeezing sickness into a short window at the very end of life. Forty three years and 204 countries of data later, that is not the pattern in the numbers. In most places illness is spreading across more of adult life, close to what the epidemiologist Ernest Gruenberg predicted in 1977 in a paper called The Failures of Success: medicine that postpones death without curing the disease behind it.

The country with the widest gap shows the trend inside its own borders too. A county level study covering 2009 to 2019 found that United States life expectancy rose half a year, to 79.1, while healthy life expectancy fell over the same decade, down 0.3 years to 66.2. The sharpest declines were among American Indian and Alaska Native populations in the western United States.

Your Pension Depends on Kids You Did Not Have made the sustainability case with dependency ratios: more retirees drawing on fewer workers. This data sharpens that case rather than repeating it. The extra years a pay-as-you-go pension is now funding are disproportionately sick years, the kind layered with disability payments and long term care costs on top of an ordinary pension check, not extra years of healthy retirement quietly costing the same as always. A system already strained by a rising dependency ratio is being asked to fund more expensive years per retiree at the same time.

Before treating a rising life expectancy number as good news on its own, check whether healthy life expectancy is rising at the same pace. In most countries it is not, and the gap is a bill someone eventually pays, in care costs or in pension costs.

content_html_zh:
全球预期寿命持续上升。 健康预期寿命并没有跟上，自 1990 年以来，204 个国家中有 203 个国家的健康预期寿命之间的差距有所扩大。

活得更长被视为一种明确的胜利。 最新的全球健康数据显示，这些额外的岁月中有越来越多的人生病了，人们的寿命和保持健康的时间之间的差距越来越大，而不是越来越好。

研究人员将其称为发病率差距：预期寿命减去健康预期寿命，即一个人没有严重疾病或残疾的预期寿命。 1990 年至 2023 年间，全球预期寿命从 64.6 岁上升至 73.8 岁。 健康预期寿命也有所增长，但速度较慢，从 55.9 岁增至 63.1 岁。 患病年数与死亡年数或健康年数之差从 8.8 年增加到 10.7 年，增加了近 22%。

对于一个不幸的国家来说，这并不是一个四舍五入的错误。 在所研究的 204 个国家和地区中，有 203 个国家和地区的差距在扩大，并且贯穿整个成年人的生命周期，而不仅仅是最后几年。

  • 全球一生中健康状况不佳的比例从 1990 年的 13.6% 上升到 2023 年的 14.5%
  • 女性健康状况不佳的差距比男性更大，平均为 12.1 年，而男性则为 9.3 年
  • 2023年差距最大的三个国家属于富裕国家：美国为14年，澳大利亚为13.9年，加拿大为13.7年

病因并非少数罕见疾病。 由腰痛、抑郁和焦虑、年龄相关的听力损失、跌倒以及一系列其他慢性非致命疾病引起的肌肉骨骼疾病合计占全球所有不健康年份的 57%。 现代医学非常擅长让心脏病发作、癌症诊断或中风的人存活下来。 它对于预防随后出现并永久存在的慢性疾病的效果要差得多。

1980 年，医生 James Fries 提出了相反的结果。 他的发病率压缩假说预测，健康的习惯推迟疾病发作的速度比推迟死亡的速度要快，从而将疾病压缩到生命的最后阶段。 经过 43 年和 204 个国家的数据，这并不是数字的模式。 在大多数地方，疾病在成年人的生活中蔓延，这与流行病学家欧内斯特·格伦伯格 (Ernest Gruenberg) 1977 年在一篇名为《成功的失败：药物推迟死亡而不治愈死亡背后的疾病》的论文中所预测的情况接近。

差距最大的国家在其国内也显示出这种趋势。 一项涵盖 2009 年至 2019 年的县级研究发现，美国的预期寿命增加了半年，达到 79.1 岁，而健康预期寿命在同一十年中下降了 0.3 年，降至 66.2 岁。 下降幅度最大的是美国西部的美洲印第安人和阿拉斯加原住民人口。

你的养老金取决于你没有的孩子，用抚养比来说明可持续发展的理由：更多的退休人员依靠更少的工人。 这些数据使这一情况变得更加尖锐，而不是重复它。 现收现付养老金现在资助的额外年限是不成比例的患病年限，即在普通养老金支票之上叠加伤残津贴和长期护理费用的年限，而不是像往常一样悄然花费同样费用的额外年限的健康退休金。 一个已经因赡养率上升而紧张的系统被要求同时为每个退休人员提供更昂贵的年费。

在将预期寿命数字的上升本身视为好消息之前，先检查一下健康预期寿命是否也在以同样的速度增长。 在大多数国家，情况并非如此，这个缺口是某人最终要支付的账单，包括护理费用或养老金费用。
